title: Cheers Restore Review: Does It Work? Side Effects, Reddit and Value
excerpt: An honest Cheers Restore review: what the DHM and L-cysteine research actually shows, side effects and medication cautions, what Reddit users say, and whether it's worth the price.
metaDescription: Honest Cheers Restore review: does the DHM + L-cysteine formula work, side effects, what Reddit users say, and whether it's worth about $3 a serving.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Cheers Restore is a well-made, clearly labeled DHM supplement from a real company, and plenty of people say it helps them feel better the morning after drinking. But it is not a proven hangover cure. Its two headline ingredients, DHM (dihydromyricetin, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree) and L-cysteine (an amino acid), each have some research behind them, mostly small or early-stage. And you pay a premium for the Cheers name. If you like the all-in-one convenience and the price doesn't bother you, it's a reasonable choice. If you mainly want the DHM, you can get the same ingredient for a fraction of the cost from a plain DHM brand.

**Who it suits:** occasional social drinkers who want one product that combines DHM with a few supporting ingredients and don't mind paying around three dollars a serving. **Who should skip it:** anyone on a tight budget, anyone who drinks heavily or often (no supplement fixes that), and anyone taking sedatives or other prescription medicines without first checking with a doctor or pharmacist.

> **This is not medical advice.** This review explains published research and the company's own descriptions of its product. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Cheers Restore is a dietary supplement, not a drug. It has not been approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and it does not lower your blood alcohol, make you sober, or make it safe to drive. **Ask a doctor or pharmacist first if** you take prescription medicine (especially sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety medication, or blood thinners), are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have liver or kidney disease. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or can't be woken up, call 911.

**About our relationship with Cheers:** we don't have an affiliate arrangement with Cheers Health, so this review doesn't link to their store and we earn nothing if you buy it. We do earn a commission on a couple of the DHM products mentioned near the end, and we say so where they appear.

## What Cheers Restore Is

Cheers Restore is the flagship product from Cheers Health, a US supplement company. The brand started out under the name Thrive+ and picked up early attention from an appearance on the TV show Shark Tank before rebranding as Cheers. Its pitch is simple: take a few capsules when you drink, and wake up feeling more like yourself.

The product is a capsule supplement built around DHM. Cheers describes its formula as a patented combination of DHM and L-cysteine, with supporting ingredients. Depending on the version and the retailer listing, those supporting ingredients have included things like milk thistle, prickly pear, ginger, vine tea extract, electrolytes, and B vitamins.

One honest caution before we go further: the exact amounts in Cheers Restore have been reported differently in different places over the years, including on our own older comparison pages. Supplement companies reformulate, and listings on retail sites can lag behind the current bottle. **The label on the bottle in your hand is the only number that counts.** Check the Supplement Facts panel for the amount of DHM and L-cysteine per serving and how many capsules make up a serving before you compare it with anything else.

## Does Cheers Restore Work? The Ingredient Evidence

There is no large, independent, published clinical trial of Cheers Restore itself as a finished product. So the fair way to judge it is to look at what's known about its main ingredients, then be clear about the gap between "an ingredient has interesting research" and "this pill will fix your hangover."

### DHM: promising, mostly from animal research

DHM is the ingredient that most of the interest centers on. The best-known study is a 2012 paper in the *Journal of Neuroscience* from a research team at UCLA. In rats, DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal. The proposed mechanism involves GABA-A receptors, the brain receptors that alcohol acts on to cause its sedating, wobbly effects. In plain words, DHM appeared to blunt some of alcohol's effects on those receptors.

Later animal studies, including work from researchers at the University of Southern California, looked at DHM and the liver. In mice fed alcohol, DHM was linked to less fat buildup in the liver and changes in how alcohol and its by-products were processed. That research is part of why DHM gets marketed for "liver support."

Here's the important part: **these were animal studies.** Rats and mice process alcohol differently from people, and they were given doses scaled to their body size in controlled lab conditions. Good human trials of DHM for hangovers are still scarce, and the ones that exist are small. That doesn't mean DHM doesn't work. It means the evidence is promising but not settled, and anyone who tells you DHM is "clinically proven" to prevent hangovers is overselling it.

DHM also has a known weakness: it isn't absorbed very well when you swallow it. Much of what you take may never reach your bloodstream. Researchers have been working on ways to improve this, but for a standard capsule it's a reasonable question how much of the dose actually does anything.

For a deeper look at the whole body of research, including what's still missing, see our [honest review of the DHM science](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025).

### L-cysteine: one small but real human trial

L-cysteine is the more interesting half of the Cheers pitch, because it has at least one controlled human study directly on hangovers. A 2020 study published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* by researchers in Finland tested L-cysteine against a placebo in a small group of healthy young men who drank a set amount of alcohol. The researchers reported that L-cysteine reduced some hangover symptoms, particularly nausea and headache, compared with placebo.

The idea behind it makes sense. When your body breaks down alcohol, it first makes **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound linked to nausea, headache, and a racing heart. L-cysteine is thought to help bind acetaldehyde and is also a building block for glutathione, one of the body's main antioxidants.

The limits are just as important. The study was small, it only included young men, and it hasn't been widely repeated by independent groups. It tested L-cysteine on its own, not combined with DHM. One study is a reason to be interested, not proof.

### The supporting ingredients

The rest of the formula is a mix of ingredients with varying amounts of evidence:

- **Milk thistle** is the most studied liver herb. Human results for liver conditions are mixed, and there's no strong evidence it prevents hangovers.
- **Prickly pear** extract got attention from a small study published in the early 2000s that suggested it might ease some hangover symptoms, possibly by reducing inflammation. It hasn't been well confirmed since.
- **Ginger** has fairly good evidence for nausea in general (for example, in pregnancy and motion sickness), so it's a sensible inclusion if nausea is your main hangover symptom.
- **B vitamins and electrolytes** can help if you're low in them, but they don't prevent the core causes of a hangover. Drinking water and eating do much of the same job.

### Does the combination add up?

Cheers argues that DHM and L-cysteine work on different parts of the problem, so combining them makes sense. That's a reasonable theory. DHM is thought to work mainly on the brain side and possibly the liver, while L-cysteine targets acetaldehyde. But "two ingredients with some evidence" isn't the same as "a combination proven to work better." We haven't seen strong independent research testing the combination head to head against either ingredient alone, or against placebo.

### What the ingredients can't do

No matter how good the formula is, there are things it won't change:

- **It won't lower your blood alcohol.** You'll be just as impaired. Never use it as a reason to drive.
- **It won't undo heavy drinking.** The amount you drink is still the biggest factor in how bad you feel. A 2019 crossover trial from Witten/Herdecke University in Germany, best known for testing the "beer before liquor" saying, found that the order of drinks made little difference. How much people drank and how they felt while drinking mattered far more.
- **It won't fix dehydration or poor sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep and makes you lose fluid. Water, food, and sleep still do a lot of the work.

**Our take on "does it work":** some of the ingredients have real but limited evidence, the dose of each varies by version, and the product itself hasn't been independently proven. Many users report a noticeable benefit, and some of that may be the ingredients and some may be the placebo effect plus drinking a little more carefully when you've taken a "hangover pill." It's a reasonable thing to try. It's not a guarantee.

## Cheers Restore Side Effects and Safety

Cheers Restore is generally well tolerated based on what's known about its ingredients and on user reports. Serious side effects appear to be uncommon. But "natural" doesn't mean free of risk, and a few points deserve attention.

### Possible side effects

- **Drowsiness or grogginess.** Because DHM appears to act on the same GABA-A receptors involved in relaxation and sleep, some people report feeling sleepy after taking DHM products. That's usually not a problem after a night out, but it's worth knowing.
- **Stomach upset.** Some people get mild nausea, bloating, or loose stools, especially when taking several capsules on an empty stomach. L-cysteine and ginger can both cause stomach discomfort in some people.
- **Headache.** A few users report headaches, though it's hard to separate this from the drinking itself.
- **Allergic reactions.** Milk thistle is in the same plant family as ragweed, daisies, and marigolds. If you're allergic to those, check the label carefully.

### Medication interactions

This is the part that matters most. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking Cheers Restore if you take any prescription medicine.** A few specific concerns:

- **Sedatives, sleep aids, and anxiety medicines.** Benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, and some other drugs also act on GABA-A receptors. Combining them with DHM and alcohol hasn't been well studied, and stacking sedating effects is the kind of thing that can go wrong.
- **Drugs processed by the liver.** Lab studies suggest DHM and milk thistle may affect some liver enzymes that break down medications. The real-world significance in people isn't clear, but it's a reason to ask if you take medicine with a narrow safety margin, such as blood thinners or certain seizure or heart medications.
- **Diabetes medication.** Some animal research suggests DHM may affect blood sugar. If you manage blood sugar with medication, check first.

Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers these in more detail.

### Who should avoid it or ask first

- People who are pregnant or breastfeeding (there's no safety data, and alcohol should be avoided anyway).
- Anyone with liver or kidney disease.
- Anyone under the legal drinking age.
- Anyone who drinks heavily most days. If that's you, the most useful step is talking to a doctor about the drinking itself, not finding a better hangover pill. A supplement that makes heavy drinking feel easier can make the underlying problem easier to ignore.

## What Reddit and Other Users Say About Cheers Restore

We read through discussions about Cheers on Reddit and in customer reviews to get a fair picture. We're summarizing common themes here, not quoting individuals, and this kind of feedback is anecdotal by nature: people who had a strong experience, good or bad, are the ones most likely to post.

### What people like

- **It helps some people noticeably.** A meaningful share of users say they wake up with less headache, less nausea, and less of the foggy, drained feeling after a night of moderate drinking. Some describe it as one of the few products they've noticed a difference with.
- **Convenience.** People like having one product with several ingredients instead of buying and combining separate supplements.
- **Trust in the brand.** Cheers is a known name with clear labeling and a polished product, which some buyers find reassuring in a supplement market full of unknown brands.

### What people complain about

- **Price.** This is by far the most common complaint. Many people point out that the main ingredient, DHM, is widely available from other brands for much less.
- **Mixed results.** Plenty of users say it did nothing for them, or that it helped on light nights but not on heavy ones. Some suspect any benefit they noticed was placebo or simply from drinking water and pacing themselves.
- **Number of capsules.** A serving is multiple capsules, and some people need to take more on heavier nights, which drives the cost up further.
- **Grogginess.** Some users mention feeling sleepy or sluggish, which fits with how DHM is thought to work.

### The recurring Reddit advice

A common thread in supplement and hangover discussions is: "If you want to try DHM, try a cheap plain DHM product first. If it works for you, you've saved money. If you want the extra ingredients, then consider Cheers." We think that's sensible advice, and it matches our own pricing analysis below.

## Pricing and Value: Is Cheers Restore Worth It?

At the price we last tracked, Cheers Restore worked out to roughly **three dollars per serving** (about $35 for a 12-serving pack). Prices change often, and subscriptions, bundles, and sales can bring that down, so check the current price before buying.

Compare that with plain DHM supplements:

| | Cheers Restore | Typical plain DHM brand |
|---|---|---|
| Main ingredients | DHM, L-cysteine, plus supporting ingredients | DHM only (some add L-cysteine) |
| Rough cost per serving | About $3 | Often under $1 to about $2 |
| Brand recognition | High | Varies |
| Independent product trials | None we're aware of | None we're aware of |
| Best for | Convenience and an all-in-one formula | Value and controlling your own dose |

So the real question is whether L-cysteine, the supporting ingredients, and the brand are worth paying two to four times as much per night. For some people they are. If nausea is your main hangover symptom, the L-cysteine and ginger may be worth something to you. But if you're paying mostly for the DHM, a plain product gets you there for much less.

### The value verdict

- **Worth it if:** you drink occasionally, you like the all-in-one format, the cost per night doesn't matter much to you, and you've tried it and noticed a real difference.
- **Not worth it if:** you drink often (the cost adds up quickly), you're trying DHM for the first time and don't yet know if it helps you, or you mainly care about the DHM dose.

### Cheaper DHM alternatives

If you want to try DHM without the Cheers price, these are two options we track. **These are affiliate links: we earn a commission if you buy through them, at no extra cost to you.**

- **[Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20)** is a plain DHM supplement with a large bottle and a low cost per serving. It's the simplest way to find out whether DHM does anything for you.
- **[No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20)** pairs DHM with L-cysteine and a few supporting ingredients, so it's closer to the Cheers approach, usually at a lower cost per serving.

As with Cheers, check each label for the current dose and serving size, and the same safety advice applies to all of them.

## How to Use Cheers Restore (If You Try It)

If you decide to try it, a few practical points will help you get a fair test:

1. **Follow the label.** Cheers gives its own guidance on how many capsules to take and when. Don't take extra on the theory that more is better.
2. **Test it on a normal night.** Try it when you drink a typical amount for you, and compare how you feel with a similar night without it. One night is not much of a test, so try it a few times.
3. **Keep the basics.** Eat before and while drinking, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and stop at a reasonable point. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what actually makes the biggest difference.
4. **Watch for drowsiness.** If it makes you sleepy, take that into account, especially if you have to get up early.
5. **Don't mix with sedatives** or other medicines without checking with a doctor or pharmacist first.

If you want to understand typical DHM amounts and timing in general, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains what the research used and how people usually take it.

## Pros and Cons Summary

**Pros**

- Built around DHM and L-cysteine, two ingredients with at least some supporting research
- Clearly labeled product from an established brand
- Convenient all-in-one formula
- Generally well tolerated
- Many users report a real improvement on moderate drinking nights

**Cons**

- No independent published trial of the finished product
- Most DHM research is in animals, and human evidence is thin
- Expensive compared with plain DHM
- Multiple capsules per serving, sometimes more on heavy nights
- Results are inconsistent across users
- Possible drowsiness and medication interactions

## The Bottom Line

- Cheers Restore is a legitimate, well-labeled supplement, not a scam, but it's also not a proven hangover cure.
- The DHM research is promising but mostly from animals. The L-cysteine research includes one small human trial with encouraging results.
- Side effects appear mild and uncommon, but check with a doctor if you take any prescription medicine, especially sedatives.
- User opinions are genuinely mixed. Some people swear by it, and others notice nothing.
- At roughly three dollars a serving, you're paying a premium for the brand and convenience. If you mainly want DHM, a plain DHM product costs much less and is a cheaper way to see if it works for you.
- Whatever you take, the amount you drink matters far more than any supplement.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Cheers Restore actually work?**

It may help some people, but it isn't proven. Its main ingredients have some research behind them: DHM mostly from animal studies, and L-cysteine from one small 2020 human trial that found less nausea and headache than placebo. There's no large independent trial of Cheers Restore itself. Many users report feeling better the next morning, while others notice no difference. It won't lower your blood alcohol or undo heavy drinking.

**What are the side effects of Cheers Restore?**

Side effects appear to be uncommon and usually mild. The ones people mention most are drowsiness or grogginess (DHM is thought to act on the same brain receptors involved in relaxation), mild stomach upset, and occasionally headache. Milk thistle can trigger reactions in people allergic to ragweed and related plants. If you take prescription medicine, especially sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety medication, or blood thinners, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using it.

**Is Cheers Restore worth the money?**

It depends on how often you drink and what you're paying for. At the price we last tracked it was roughly three dollars a serving, which is two to four times what many plain DHM supplements cost. If you like the all-in-one formula and drink only occasionally, the extra cost may be fine. If you mainly want DHM, or you're trying it for the first time, a plain DHM product is a cheaper way to find out whether it helps you.

**What's in Cheers Restore?**

Cheers describes its formula as a patented combination of DHM and L-cysteine. Versions and retail listings have also included supporting ingredients such as milk thistle, prickly pear, ginger, vine tea extract, electrolytes, and B vitamins. Amounts have been reported differently over the years, so check the Supplement Facts panel on your bottle for the current dose and serving size.

**Is Cheers Restore better than plain DHM?**

Not clearly. Cheers adds L-cysteine and supporting ingredients, and L-cysteine has one small human study suggesting it may ease nausea and headache. But no independent research has shown the Cheers combination works better than DHM alone. Plain DHM costs much less, so many people try it first and only move to a multi-ingredient product if they want the extras.

**What does Reddit say about Cheers Restore?**

Opinions are genuinely mixed. Common positives are that it helps some people feel noticeably better after moderate drinking and that the all-in-one format is convenient. The most common complaints are the price, inconsistent results (some notice nothing, or only on light nights), the number of capsules, and grogginess. A frequent piece of advice is to try a cheap plain DHM product first before paying more for Cheers.

**Can I take Cheers Restore with medication?**

Ask a doctor or pharmacist first. DHM appears to act on GABA-A receptors, the same targets as benzodiazepines and many sleep aids, so combining it with sedatives and alcohol is a concern. Lab research also suggests DHM and milk thistle may affect liver enzymes that break down some medicines. The real-world effect isn't well understood, which is a reason to check rather than assume it's fine.

**Was Cheers on Shark Tank?**

The company behind Cheers originally sold its product under the name Thrive+ and appeared on Shark Tank before rebranding as Cheers. A TV appearance says nothing about whether a supplement works, so judge it on its ingredients, label, and price rather than the publicity.
